publisher: American Psychological Association (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology)
table: Results, 'Trajectories of grief': the five patterns of depression (CES-D) from preloss to 18 months postloss
title: Bonanno GA, Wortman CB, Lehman DR, Tweed RG, Haring M, Sonnega J, Carr D, Nesse RM. Resilience to loss and chronic grief: a prospective study from preloss to 18-months postloss. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 83(5):1150-1164, 2002.
universe: 205 married older adults in the Changing Lives of Older Couples study who lost a spouse; mean age 72 (SD 6.5). 185 (90.2 percent) fell into the five patterns below.
limits: One loss type (death of a spouse), one age group (older adults), one metro area, depression symptoms (CES-D, converted to z-scores) rather than a mood scale. It calibrates the band of how many bereaved people recover, never one person's outcome. Three patterns under 5 percent of the sample (delayed grief 8, delayed-improved 10, improved-relapsed 2) are listed but were not used by the authors for their main analyses.

patterns.meaning: Low depression before and after the loss, with no lasting rise.
Low depression before the loss, high after it, still high at 18 months.
Low depression before the loss, high at 6 months, back to low by 18 months.
High depression before the loss, lower after it.
High depression before and after the loss.
Low before and at 6 months, high at 18 months.
High before, higher at 6 months, lower at 18 months.
High before, lower at 6 months, high again at 18 months.

highDepressionCutoff: 80th percentile of preloss CES-D z-scores; 49 high-baseline participants (M 1.61, SD 0.88), 156 low-baseline (M -0.39, SD 0.57).

quotes: As anticipated, most of the sample (n = 185; 90.2%) were captured by five conceptually relevant patterns: common grief (n = 22; 10.7%); chronic grief (n = 32; 15.6%); resilient (n = 94; 45.9%); chronic depression (n = 16; 7.8%); and depressed-improved (n = 21; 10.2%).
the remaining 20 participants (9.8%) were spread sparsely across the delayed grief (n = 8; 3.9%), delayed-improved (n = 10; 4.9%), and improved-relapsed (n = 2; 1.0%) patterns.
